Posted September 2, 2005
Analysis by Richard Cowan

Even something as utterly detached from reality as the drugwar does not operate in a vacuum. During the Bush administration several important events have changed the global context for the development of the international prohibitionist police state.

First, Bush repudiated several treaties, implicitly undermining the notion that the world was inescapably committed to prohibitionism by sacred commitments.
From May of 2001, see
 Bush Changes the Global Climate for Marijuana Prohibition. Analysis by Richard Cowan

Then came September 11, which so distracted the nation that it was difficult to get a discussion of other issues. The drugwarriors, however, could not resist exploiting the tragedy, which raised the issue again in a way that offended far more people than it convinced.
From December of 2001, see
 The Endless Cynicism of the Drug Warriors. The Drug War and Terrorism. MarijuanaNews Analysis by Richard Cowan

The invasion of Afghanistan was popular and somewhat successful, but it created new facts on the ground  to use an old Communist phrase  in the form of booming poppy production by our allies there. Most of it is being shipped to our allies in Europe, where the surge in cheap heroin put even more pressure on governments to provide addicts with alternatives to the black market. That is heresy to the prohibitionist ideologues.
From August of 2002, see
 Afghan Opium Crop Booms Under DEAland Control As Feds Focus On Cannabis, Reverse Policy On Prosecuting Small Medical Growers In Washington State; Cut 6 Plants In California; Seize Bongs In Illinois.

Of course, the invasion of Iraq had the effect of isolating the US and the drugwar has been increasingly viewed as American.
From March of 2003, see
 Unintended Consequences: How The Iraq War Has Changed the Global Climate for Cannabis Prohibition. Analysis by Richard Cowan  

As more and more people questioned the stated reasons for the invasion and the disastrous state of affairs in liberated Iraq, Bushs popularity and credibility have plunged. One wonders how long it will be before the so-called anti-war movement begins to question whether it is also wrong to lie to justify a war on our own people.
From July of 2003, see
 Embarrassing Questions: If It Was Wrong to Lie to Justify the War on Saddam, Why Isnt It Wrong to Lie to Justify the War on Cannabis Users? Analysis by Richard Cowan
From April of 2004, see
 Bush Should Have John  Comical Ali  Walters Explain The Iraq War, Then The Media Would Never Ask Any Embarrassing Questions. Doctrine Of Drug Czar Infallibility? Blame Canada, Again.

More recently, increasing violence on both sides of the Mexican border and the fact that we have simply lost control over both human and contraband traffic provoked an outcry across the political spectrum. Amazingly, on August 29th, Pat Buchanan actually called for Bush to be impeached for his failure to enforce the laws controlling immigration. He was writing on the religious right website World Net Daily.

Two days later, Joseph Farah, the World Net Daily publisher, echoed his call.  Farah claims, al-Qaida operatives have already used the open Mexican border not only to sneak operatives into the country but to smuggle in nuclear weapons with the help of the MS-13 (Mara Salvatrucha) street gang.

Of course, neither Buchanan nor Farah recognize the damage being done to Mexico by DEAlands drugwar or the burden that marijuana prohibition in particular places on our border control system. However, there was increasing media coverage of drugwar violence on the Mexican side of the border, especially in Nuevo Laredo, which I called Baghdad on the Border.
From June, see
 Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report June 20, 2005 Boje Freed On Bail. Baghdad on the Border Occupied. Use Highest in College Towns. Internet Addictive; Vaporization? Dont Tell GW.

Now the tragic events in New Orleans are creating a new context that may very well challenge the entire American political system, even the sacred and eternal drugwar.

Presumably, in the next few days law and order will be restored to New Orleans and the poor people there will be rescued from their misery, but the damage is done. Bush will be busy looking concerned and Presidential; however the phrase too little, too late has never seemed more apt. Naturally, the politicians will be playing the blame game, and there is plenty of blame to go around.

The fact is that both parties and all recent Presidents have ignored repeated warnings that New Orleans was very vulnerable to being flooded by an overdue hurricane. One can debate whether the federal government should have been able to prevent the attacks of 9/11, but there have multiple published warnings and even television programs about the danger to the City that Care Forgot. (How bitterly ironic that name now seems.)

The chaos in the flooded city is indicative of a systemic failure. In April of 1986, the Chernobyl disaster hastened the end of the Soviet system by revealing failures that could no longer be hidden. In almost every way, the situation in New Orleans is even worse.

It could not escape anyones notice that most of the people left behind were poor blacks, who are usually the people left behind. New Orleans has always been both the best and the worst of the Old South: elegance and racism, joy and grinding poverty, side by side. As in the rest of America, the best is promoted for tourism and the worst is hidden from sight. That is just human nature, but while the lights may be out in New Orleans, some things we did not want to see are more visible than ever.

While poverty kept most of those trapped from fleeing, the fact is that the black underclass is also profoundly alienated from the system. They are the primary victims of the chaos caused by drugwar and citys notoriously corrupt police department.
From April, 2004, see
 The Theory and Practice of Chaos  Analysis By Richard Cowan  
and
New Orleans Police Say That It Wasnt The Benadryl, Or The Heart Condition, Or The Kidney Failure, Or The Dehydration, Or The "Extremely Low Blood Pressure." No, It Was The Marijuana That Caused The Bus Accident! But That Contradicts The FDA

Consequently, when an evacuation order is given, they are the least likely to believe it is really necessary. "Injustice breeds injustice, bad laws breed contempt, and dispossession breeds alienation.
See
 New Zealanders Analysis of the Consequences of the Violence of Marijuana Prohibition. Bravo!
 
Indeed, many of them were undoubtedly afraid to leave their homes for fear of having it looted. They knew that they could not count on the system to protect them, because looting in poor neighborhoods seldom makes the news.

Despite its systemic challenge, the blowback from the anarchy in New Orleans will rightly hit Bush the hardest, for a variety of reasons.

First, it happened on his watch, and he was embarrassingly slow to react, callously flying off to a fundraiser in California as the storm hit the Gulf.

Second, there are simply too many echoes of the situation in Iraq, and Baghdad especially. In the midst of the horror at home perhaps a thousand Iraqi Shia pilgrims, most women and children, died in an accident in Baghdad. Of course, the anarchy in the Iraqi capital began when the Bush Administration completely failed to anticipate the consequences of abolishing the Iraqi military and the ruling party.     

The Morale of the Troops

While complaints from those on the ground in Gulf states are being heard, no one seems to have realized yet how damaging this fiasco must be to the morale of our troops in Iraq. Many of them are there unwillingly, having been in National Guard units from the very areas that have been hit the hardest. They are even less able to find out what happened to their loved ones back home.

If it is heartbreaking for any American to see what is happening, it must be truly agonizing and infuriating for the troops in Iraq who know that they and their helicopters and mobile hospitals, etc, should be at home rescuing their friends and family.

After 9/11 Bush distracted the American people by going in search of enemies, but that seems unlikely to work this time. For Bush and the entire political class, the bad news will be that the American people must recognize the bitter truth of Walt Kellys famous line from Pogo: We Have Met The Enemy and He Is Us.
